questions.q: How fast does Dawn's ion engine throw out its xenon?
questions.do: Read the first row of the Dawn, re-derived card, Exhaust speed (3,100 s × g).
questions.a: 30.4 km/s. That is about ten times faster than the hot gas from a chemical rocket (about 3 km/s).

questions.q: For a change in speed of 5 km/s, how much propellant does each engine need?
questions.do: Drag the Change in speed wanted slider to 5.00 km/s. Read the ION and CHEMICAL labels on the chart.
questions.a: Ion: about 134 kg. Chemical: about 2,929 kg, for the same 747 kg spacecraft. The chemical engine needs about 22 times more.

questions.q: How long does a spiral out of Earth orbit take, and what changes if the push is gentler?
questions.do: In Spiral out of Earth orbit, keep the push at 1.0 mm/s² and press Fly the spiral. Then drag the push slider fully left (100 µm/s²) and press Fly the spiral again.
questions.a: At 1.0 mm/s²: about 81 days, 345 laps and 7.03 km/s of speed change. At 100 µm/s²: about 2.3 years, 3,452 laps and 7.31 km/s. One quick chemical burn would need only 3.18 km/s.

questions.q: Why could Dawn stop and orbit two worlds when a chemical spacecraft could only fly past?
questions.do: Read the verdict box in the Dawn, re-derived card.
questions.a: A chemical spacecraft as heavy as Dawn would need about 28,300 kg of propellant for the same 11.49 km/s. That is 67 times the 425 kg of xenon Dawn carried. Each kilogram of xenon gives about ten times the push, so Dawn had enough to stop at Vesta and then Ceres.

questions.q: Who worked out the limit for a slow spiral escape, and when? What does the limit say?
questions.do: Read the verdict under the spiral and the third row of the Checks table.
questions.a: T. N. Edelbaum, in 1961. The gentler the push, the closer the speed change gets to the whole starting orbital speed. From a 400 km orbit that is 7.67 km/s; the lab gets 7.03 km/s at 1 mm/s².
